abstract: Object-specific variables are entangled in sensory input. For example, lightness, whether a surface is white or black, not only depends on the surface reflectance but also on the incident illumination. The brain must thus perform inference to achieve a reliable percept of lightness irrespective of illumination (lightness constancy). Whether this results from simple luminance contrast operations early in the visual system or computations at higher levels remains unresolved. We find that neural lightness signals only appear in the extragranular layers of cortical Area V4, and dominate for shadow regions, as opposed to the comparison of local and surrounding luminance (simultaneous contrast). This suggests that lightness is computed downstream from simultaneous contrast, ruling out simple low-level mechanisms, and instead supporting mid-level anchoring theory.
